newsitem.title: USA: Clinton names commission to monitor health care.
newsitem.headline: Clinton names commission to monitor health care.

text.p: Saying many Americans are worried that their medical care is suffering as costs are cut, President Clinton named a commission Wednesday to monitor health care quality and write a consumer's "bill of rights."
But there was skepticism among Republicans on Capitol Hill with one saying the commission was nothing more than a cover for health care regulations the White House wants to impose.

Clinton said the 32-member commission must work to make sure that dramatic changes in the U.S. health care industry, especially the trend toward managed care health plans, do not keep professionals from offering the best care to patients.

"In this time of transition, many Americans worry that lower costs mean lower quality and less attention to their rights," the president said in an East Room ceremony, with the new members of the commission seated on either side of him.
Usually managed care plans give patients good care and greater choice at lower cost, he said. "Managed care managed well can be the best deal for our families."
But he added: "Whether they have traditional health care or managed care, none of our people should ever have inferior care."

Under traditional "fee-for-service" health plans, people had few limits on their health care and billed their insurance providers for the costs. Managed care plans, in contrast, seek to hold down costs by controlling the care patients receive.

Clinton, who tried but failed to reform the U.S. health care system and pass universal coverage during his first term, asked the panel to move quickly to write a consumer's bill of rights, and offered them some ideas.
Doctors must be free to provide the best medical advice available and not be subject to "inappropriate" financial incentives to limit their care, Clinton said.

Consumers should also have the right to basic information about their plan and be able to resolve insurance coverage disputes simply, he said. And the elderly and disabled must receive the best care available, the president said.

Although the commission's recommendations would not be legally binding, some Republicans were wary, fearing it was another attempt to impose greater government regulation on health care like Clinton's first-term efforts, which were led by his wife, Hillary Rodham Clinton.

"Today's announcement is a politically-inspired gimmick designed to ratify the regulations President Clinton plans to impose on the private health care marketplace," Rep. Bill Thomas, Republican of California, said in a statement.

"For example, the president has already proposed allowing the government to dictate the appropriate length of hospital stays," said Thomas, who chairs the health subcommittee of the House Ways and Means Committee.
But health advocacy groups generally welcomed the new panel, which included members from business, labor, health care providers, insurers and consumer groups.
The White House stressed the intent was not to attack managed care, such as health maintenance organizations.

"A lot of people want to make this into, you know, HMO-bashing or managed-care bashing. That is not the intent. The president believes very, very strongly that good managed care can actually not only be cost-effective, but actually improve health care outcomes," said White House aide Chris Jennings.
The commission, chaired by the secretaries of Health and Human Services and Labor, was required to make a preliminary report to Clinton next Janaury and the final one next March.
